summary: RTP allows header extensions, but it was hard to use many of them. This document provides a general mechanism for using a small number of small extensions in each RTP packet, where many extensions are possible and registration is decentralized. Which ones are in use is negotiated per session.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP carries audio and video. Sometimes a sender needs to add a little extra information to each packet, such as a capture timestamp. This document defines how several such pieces can travel together in one packet without colliding, and how the two ends agree beforehand on what each piece means. The details of each piece are agreed in the session setup, not in the packet itself.

subtitle: A way to carry several small pieces of extra information in each RTP packet.

tldr.problem: The original RTP header extension allowed only one extension per packet and gave no guidance on how the 16-bit identifiers should be allocated, so extensions collided.
tldr.mechanism: The extension is now a sequence of small elements, each with a local identifier and a length, and the identifiers are mapped to names by URI out of band, usually in the session description.
tldr.outcome: This obsoletes RFC 5285 and lifts its ban on mixing one-byte and two-byte headers in the same stream, when the participants agree to it in the session description.

today: RFC 8285 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current definition of the RTP header extension format. It replaced RFC 5285, which defined the same one-byte and two-byte forms but did not allow a stream to mix them.

sections.title: The Problem With the Original Extension
sections.content:
The RTP specification RFC 3550 provides a capability to extend the RTP header, and Section 5.3.1 of that document defines the header extension format and rules for its use. The existing header extension method permits at most one extension per RTP packet, identified by a 16-bit identifier and a 16-bit length field specifying the length of the header extension in 32-bit words.

This mechanism has two conspicuous drawbacks. First, it permits only one header extension in a single RTP packet. Second, the specification gives no guidance as to how the 16-bit header extension identifiers are allocated to avoid collisions.

This specification removes the first drawback by defining a backward-compatible and extensible means to carry multiple header extension elements in a single RTP packet. It removes the second drawback by defining that these extension elements are named by URIs, defining an IANA registry for extension elements defined in IETF specifications, and providing a Session Description Protocol method for mapping between the naming URIs and the identifier values carried in the RTP packets. The header extension applies to RTP/AVP, the Audio/Visual Profile, and its extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The original design allowed one extra block per packet and left it to everyone to pick different numbers for their own blocks, so two unrelated blocks could end up with the same number. This document allows many blocks per packet and names them with web-style addresses so that two blocks can never be confused.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The goal of this design is to provide a simple mechanism whereby multiple identified extensions can be used in RTP packets, without the need for formal registration of those extensions but nonetheless avoiding collisions.

The mechanism provides an alternative to the practice of burying associated metadata into the media format bitstream. This has often been done in media data sent over fixed-bandwidth channels. Once this is done, a decoder for the specific media format needs to extract the metadata. Also, depending on the media format, the metadata can be added at the time of encoding the media so that the bit-rate used for the metadata is taken into account, but the metadata can be unknown at that time, and inserting metadata at a later time can cause a decode and re-encode to meet bit-rate requirements.

In some cases a more appropriate and higher-level mechanism may be available, and if so it can be used. For cases where a higher-level mechanism is not available, it is better to provide a mechanism at the RTP level than to have the metadata tied to a specific form of media data.
sections.plainLanguage: The aim is to carry small facts about a call next to the media, rather than hiding them inside the encoded audio or video, where only one kind of decoder could find them. The facts themselves are not defined here; each one is defined by whoever invents it.

sections.title: The One-Byte and Two-Byte Headers
sections.content:
The RTP header extension is formed as a sequence of extension elements, with possible padding. Each extension element has a local identifier and a length. The local identifiers MAY be mapped to a larger namespace in the negotiation. There are no static allocations of local identifiers, each distinct extension MUST have a unique ID, and the ID value 0 is reserved for padding and MUST NOT be used as a local identifier. An extension element with an ID of 0 MUST NOT have a length field greater than 0; if such an element is encountered, its length field MUST be ignored and processing of the entire extension MUST terminate at that point.

Since it is expected that the number of extensions in any given RTP session is small and the extensions themselves are small, the one-byte header form is preferred and MUST be supported by all receivers. In that form the 16-bit value required by the RTP specification, labeled there as the defined by profile field, MUST have the fixed bit pattern 0xBEDE. Each element starts with one byte holding a 4-bit ID in the range 1 to 14 and a 4-bit length. The length is the number, minus one, of data bytes that follow, so a value of zero means one byte of data follows and a value of 15 means 16 bytes of data. The value 15 as an identifier is reserved for a future extension and MUST NOT be used.

In the two-byte header form the defined by profile value is 0x100 followed by a 4-bit appbits field that is application dependent. For signaling, that field is treated as a special extension value assigned to local identifier 256. Each element starts with an 8-bit ID in the range 1 to 255 and an 8-bit length that gives the length of extension data in bytes, where zero means there is no subsequent data. There is one ID space for both forms, so the lower values 1 to 14 mean the same thing in each.

Padding bytes have the value of 0 and may be placed between elements or after the last one. A padding byte supplies neither an ID nor a length, and is ignored by the parser. The whole extension is parsed byte by byte with no alignment needed, and parsing stops at the end of the extension or, in the one-byte-only case, on encountering an identifier of 15. The RTP specification states that RTP is designed so that the header extension may be ignored by other interoperating implementations that have not been extended, so a header extension MUST NOT change the meaning of the standard RTP header fields or of RTCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra space in a packet is filled with small blocks. Each block starts with a number saying what it is and how long it is, followed by its data. There are two block formats: a compact one where the number and the length share a single byte, and a larger one where each gets a full byte. Padding bytes with the value zero fill any leftover room.

sections.title: Signalling Extensions With SDP
sections.content:
The indication of the presence of this extension, and the mapping of local identifiers used in the header extension to a larger namespace, MUST be performed out of band, for example as part of an SDP Offer/Answer. A usable mapping MUST use IDs in the valid range, and each ID in this range MUST be used only once for each media section, or only once if the mappings are session level. Mappings that do not conform to these rules MAY be presented, for instance during negotiation, but remapping to conformant values is necessary before they can be applied.

Each extension is named by a URI. That URI MUST be absolute, and it precisely identifies the format and meaning of the extension. URIs that contain a domain name SHOULD also contain a month-date in the form mmyyyy, and the definition of the element and assignment of the URI MUST have been authorized by the owner of the domain name on or very close to that date, which avoids problems when domain names change ownership. If the resource or document defines several extensions, the URI MUST identify the actual extension in use, for example using a fragment or query identifier.

For extensions defined in RFCs, the URI used SHOULD be a URN starting with urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext: followed by a registered, descriptive name. The mapping is carried in an attribute of the form a=extmap:<value>["/"<direction>] <URI> <extensionattributes>, where the value is the local identifier and the direction is one of sendonly, recvonly, sendrecv or inactive. The mapping MAY be provided per media stream or globally for all streams, but the definitions MUST be either all session level or all media level.

When SDP signaling is used for the RTP session, it is the presence of the extmap attributes that is diagnostic that this style of header extensions is used, not the magic number, BEDE or 100, indicated above.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends agree in advance, in the session description, which number carries which piece of information. Each piece has an absolute web-style name that says what it contains, so two different pieces can never share a number. The name usually includes the month and year so that the domain owner has approved it.

sections.title: Mixing One-Byte and Two-Byte Headers
sections.content:
To allow for backward interoperability with systems that do not support mixing one-byte and two-byte header extensions, the document defines the a=extmap-allow-mixed Session Description Protocol attribute to indicate whether the participant is capable of supporting this mode. The attribute takes no value and can be used at the session level or the media level. A participant that proposes the use of this mode SHALL itself support the reception of mixed one-byte and two-byte header extensions.

If SDP Offer/Answer is supported and used, the negotiation for mixed one-byte and two-byte extensions MUST be negotiated using SDP Offer/Answer. In the absence of such negotiation, for example when declarative SDP is used, mixed headers MUST NOT occur unless the transmitter has some out-of-band knowledge that all potential recipients support this mode.

When doing SDP Offer/Answer, an offering client that wishes to use both one-byte and two-byte extensions MUST include the attribute in the SDP offer. If the attribute is present in the offer, the answerer that supports this mode and wishes to use it SHALL include the attribute in the answer. Where the attribute has been excluded, both clients SHALL NOT use mixed one-byte and two-byte extensions in the same RTP stream, but MAY use the one-byte or two-byte form exclusively.
sections.plainLanguage: Older systems cannot handle a stream that mixes the two block formats. So a sender that wants to mix them must say so in the session description, and the other side must agree. Without that agreement, a stream uses one format or the other, never both.

sections.title: Offer and Answer
sections.content:
The simple signaling described for the extmap attribute MAY be enhanced in an SDP Offer/Answer context to permit asymmetric behavior, that is, extensions sent in only one direction, the offer of mutually exclusive alternatives, or the offer of more extensions than can be sent in a single session.

A direction attribute MAY be included in an extmap. Without it, the direction implicitly inherits from the stream direction, or is sendrecv for session-level attributes or extensions of inactive streams. It is an error to use an extension direction incompatible with the stream direction, for example a sendonly attribute for a recvonly stream.

If an extension is marked as sendonly and the answerer desires to receive it, the extension MUST be marked as recvonly in the SDP answer. An answerer that has no desire to receive the extension, or does not understand it, SHOULD remove it from the answer. If an extension is marked as recvonly and the answerer desires to send it, the extension MUST be marked as sendonly in the answer. Local identifiers in the valid range must not be used more than once per media section, the same identifier MUST be used for the same offered extension in the answer, and identifier values in the valid range MUST NOT be altered.

If a party wishes to offer mutually exclusive alternatives, then multiple extensions with the same identifier in the extended range 4096 to 4351 MAY be offered, and the answerer SHOULD select at most one of them and remap it to a free identifier in the valid range. Similarly, if more extensions are offered than can fit in the valid range, identifiers in the range 4096 to 4351 MAY be offered and the answerer SHOULD choose those that are desired and remap them to a free identifier. The range 4096 to 4351 is deliberately restricted to allow expansion of the range of valid identifiers in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides negotiate which extensions each will send and which it will receive, and they may narrow the list from what was offered. An extension can be marked as send-only or receive-only. If there are more extensions than numbers available, the offer can use a reserved range and the receiver picks the ones it wants and renumbers them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document defines only a place to transmit information; the security implications of each of the extensions must be discussed with those extensions.

Extension usage is negotiated using SDP Offer/Answer, so integrity protection and end-to-end authentication MUST be implemented. The security considerations of the Offer/Answer model MUST be followed to prevent, for example, extension-usage blocking.

Header extensions have the same security coverage as the RTP header itself. When the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol is used to protect RTP sessions, the RTP payload can be both encrypted and integrity protected, while the RTP header is either unprotected or integrity protected. In order to prevent denial-of-service attacks, for example by changing the header extension, integrity protection SHOULD be used. Lower-layer security protection such as Datagram Transport Layer Security MAY be used. RTP header extensions can carry sensitive information for which participants in multimedia sessions want confidentiality, and RFC 6904 provides a mechanism that extends the mechanisms of SRTP to selectively encrypt RTP header extensions in SRTP.
sections.plainLanguage: This document does not decide how safe a particular extension is; the extension's own specification must do that. The rules here are about the transport: the session setup must be protected, and the packets should be integrity protected so that a middlebox cannot rewrite the extension.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 5285
sections.content:
The major motivation for updating RFC 5285 was to allow having one-byte and two-byte RTP header extensions in the same RTP stream, but not in the same RTP packet. The support for this case is negotiated using the new SDP attribute extmap-allow-mixed specified in this document.

The other major change is to update the requirement from the RTP specifications that the header extension is designed so that the header extension may be ignored. More text was added to the section on transmission considerations to clarify when and how many times to send the RTP header extension to provide a higher probability of delivery. The Security Considerations section was expanded, and the rest of the changes are editorial.
sections.plainLanguage: The headline change is that a single stream may now carry both kinds of block, as long as both ends have agreed to it. The document also spells out the rule that a receiver that does not understand an extension must be able to ignore it, and it adds more guidance on how often to repeat the extension so that it gets through.

fields.name: ID
fields.desc: Local identifier of this element, in the range 1 to 14. The value 15 is reserved.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Number of data bytes minus one, so 0 means one byte of data and 15 means 16 bytes.

fields.name: ID
fields.desc: Local identifier of this element, in the range 1 to 255.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the extension data in bytes, not counting the ID and length fields. Zero means no data.

data.title: extmap grammar
data.code:
extmap-value = mapentry SP extensionname
               [SP extensionattributes]

mapentry = "extmap:" 1*5DIGIT ["/" direction]

extensionname = URI

extensionattributes = byte-string

direction = "sendonly" / "recvonly" / "sendrecv" / "inactive"

messages.note: a=extmap:1 URI-toffset, a=extmap:14 URI-obscure, a=extmap:4096 URI-gps-string.

messages.label: SDP ANSWER
messages.note: a=extmap:2/recvonly URI-gps-string on video, a=extmap:1/sendonly URI-toffset on audio.
